claims.claim: The Psalter has 150 psalms in five books (1–41, 42–72, 73–89, 90–106, 107–150), each of the first four ending with a doxology.
Greek/Latin numbering usually runs one behind the Hebrew from Psalm 10 to 147.
claims.source: Standard; e.g. Alter, The Book of Psalms (2007), introduction

claims.claim: 73 psalms are attributed to David in the Hebrew headings; Asaph 50, 73–83; sons of Korah 42–49, 84–85, 87–88; Moses Psalm 90; Solomon 72 and 127.
Talmud Bava Batra 14b–15a: David wrote the Psalms with ten elders including Adam, Abraham and Moses.
11QPs-a credits David with 4,050 compositions.
claims.source: 11QPs-a col. XXVII ('David's Compositions'); J. A. Sanders, DJD 4 (1965)

claims.claim: Around forty Psalms manuscripts among the Dead Sea Scrolls; Psalm 151 in some and in the Septuagint and Orthodox Bibles.
claims.source: P. W. Flint, The Dead Sea Psalms Scrolls and the Book of Psalms (1997)

claims.claim: Qur'an calls the Psalms the Zabur, given to David.
Robert Lowth's Oxford lectures on Hebrew poetry published 1753; parallelism; he later became Bishop of London.
Kugel (1981) and Alter (1985) argued the second line intensifies.
claims.source: Kugel, The Idea of Biblical Poetry (1981); Alter, The Art of Biblical Poetry (1985)

claims.claim: Gunkel's form-critical types; laments the largest single group, about a third.
claims.source: Gunkel and Begrich, Einleitung in die Psalmen (1933); Westermann, Praise and Lament (1981)

claims.claim: Athanasius, Letter to Marcellinus: the Psalms speak for us, like a mirror (paraphrased).
Calvin called the Psalms an anatomy of all the parts of the soul (paraphrased, no quotation marks).
claims.source: Calvin, Commentary on the Psalms, author's preface (1557)

claims.claim: Mishnah Tamid 7:4 lists the psalm for each day sung by the Levites.
Rule of Benedict: all 150 psalms weekly; the fathers did it in a day.
BCP reads the whole Psalter monthly; Geneva Psalter 1562; Scottish Psalter 1650.
Coverdale translated the Psalms 1535; his version is the BCP Psalter.
Handel's Messiah quotes Psalms 2, 16, 22, 24, 68; Stravinsky Symphony of Psalms 1930; Lincoln's Second Inaugural quotes Psalm 19:9.
Psalm 88 heading: sons of Korah, maskil of Heman the Ezrahite, mahalath leannoth.
claims.source: Hebrew heading of Psalm 88; 1 Chronicles 6:33; 15:19; 1 Kings 4:31

claims.claim: Psalm 88's last Hebrew word is 'darkness' (machshak).
Catholic Compline sets Psalm 88 on Fridays.
claims.source: Liturgy of the Hours (1971), Night Prayer, Friday

claims.claim: Liturgy of the Hours omits Psalms 58, 83, 109 and some verses (e.g. 137:7–9).
claims.source: General Instruction of the Liturgy of the Hours §131

claims.claim: Augustine read the 'little ones' of Psalm 137:9 as sinful desires dashed against Christ the rock.
C. S. Lewis on the cursings; Bonhoeffer on praying vengeance with Christ.
claims.source: Lewis, Reflections on the Psalms (1958) ch. 3; Bonhoeffer, Das Gebetbuch der Bibel (1940)

claims.claim: Brueggemann's orientation, disorientation, new orientation.
claims.source: Brueggemann, JSOT 17 (1980); The Message of the Psalms (1984)

claims.claim: Lamentations: five poems, four acrostics; read on Tisha B'Av.
Solomon spoke 3,000 proverbs and 1,005 songs; his wisdom excelled Egypt's.
Hezekiah's men copied proverbs; Hezekiah reigned c. 715–686 BC.
Instruction of Amenemope: BM EA 10474, published by Budge 1923–24; Erman 1924 parallels; composed c. 1300–1075 BC; thirty chapters; boundary stone and riches with wings parallels.
claims.source: Budge (1923, 1924); Erman (1924); Lichtheim, AEL II (1976); Fox, Proverbs 10–31 (2009)

claims.claim: 'Thirty' in Proverbs 22:20 reread after Amenemope.
Ptahhotep c. 2400 BC (attributed to an Old Kingdom vizier).
Proverbs 31:10–31 is an acrostic, sung as Eshet Chayil on Friday night.
Qoheleth from the root for 'assembly'; Greek Ekklesiastes; Luther 'Prediger'.
Song of Songs Rabbah 1:1:10: Song in youth, Proverbs in middle age, Ecclesiastes in old age.
Ecclesiastes dated c. 450–250 BC from late Hebrew and Persian loanwords (pardes 2:5).
Hevel appears 38 times in Ecclesiastes.
'Under the sun' about thirty times.
Whybray, 'Qoheleth, Preacher of Joy' (1982); seven enjoyment passages.
Shabbat 30b: sages sought to hide Ecclesiastes; kept because it begins and ends with Torah; Yadayim 3:5 debate.
Ecclesiastes read at Sukkot.
Jerome's commentary c. 388, recalling reading it with Blesilla.
Siduri's advice in the Old Babylonian Gilgamesh parallels Ecclesiastes 9:7–9.
claims.source: Sippar tablet (OB version) iii; A. R. George (2003)

claims.claim: Hemingway's The Sun Also Rises (1926) takes its title and epigraph from Ecclesiastes 1:4–7.
Tolstoy (1828–1910); War and Peace 1869; Anna Karenina 1878; A Confession written 1879–82, banned, printed Geneva 1884.
claims.source: Standard biographies (e.g. Rosamund Bartlett, Tolstoy: A Russian Life, 2010)

claims.claim: Aylmer Maude (1858–1938) translated A Confession, published 1921.
claims.source: Standard Ebooks colophon ('translated from Russian in 1921 by Aylmer Maude'); OUP World's Classics

claims.claim: The fable of the man in the well is Indian and came west in Barlaam and Josaphat.
claims.source: Standard; e.g. the Barlaam legend's apologue of the unicorn/man in the pit

claims.claim: Schopenhauer: life a pendulum between pain and boredom.
claims.source: World as Will and Representation I §57 (1818)

claims.claim: Camus calls suicide the one truly serious philosophical problem (paraphrase).
Schellenberg's hiddenness argument (1993).
Mother Teresa felt God's absence for most of nearly fifty years.
claims.source: Come Be My Light, ed. Kolodiejchuk (2007)

claims.claim: William James, 'Is Life Worth Living?' (1895, in The Will to Believe, 1897): mountain-leap example; belief helping make the fact.
Górecki's Symphony No. 3 (1976), second movement from words on a Gestapo cell wall.
Song of Songs mostly in the woman's voice; wasf passages 4:1–7, 5:10–16, 7:1–9.
Egyptian love songs c. 1300–1100 BC (Papyrus Chester Beatty I, Dublin; Harris 500, London; Deir el-Medina ostraca).
claims.source: Fox, The Song of Songs and the Ancient Egyptian Love Songs (1985)

claims.claim: Shalhevetyah in 8:6 may be 'flame of Yah' or 'mighty flame'.
Akiva: 'all the Writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the Holy of Holies'.
Akiva on singing the Song in banquet houses.
Targum reads the Song as Israel's history from exodus to Messiah; read on the Sabbath of Passover; some read it Friday evenings.
Origen's commentary c. 240, ten books, partly surviving in Rufinus's Latin; Jewish custom not to let the young read it.
claims.source: Origen, Commentary on the Song, prologue

claims.claim: Bernard preached 86 sermons 1135–1153, reaching only 3:1; Sermon 1: only experience teaches this song (paraphrase).
John of the Cross wrote the Spiritual Canticle in prison in Toledo, 1578.
Theodore of Mopsuestia read the Song literally.
John Paul II's theology of the body 1979–84 draws on the Song.
claims.source: Man and Woman He Created Them, audiences 108–113

claims.claim: Hosea active c. 750–725 BC; Gomer; Hosea 2:19–20 said when wrapping tefillin; Romans 9:25 quotes Hosea 2:23.
Ben Sira c. 180 BC identifies Wisdom with Torah.
Wisdom of Solomon: Greek, probably Alexandria, 1st c. BC; deuterocanonical for Catholics and Orthodox; Apocrypha for Protestants (Article VI).
claims.source: Standard introductions; BCP Articles of Religion VI

claims.claim: Apaugasma appears only in Wisdom 7:26 and Hebrews 1:3 in the Greek Bible.
Philo calls the Logos God's firstborn and image.
Genesis Rabbah 1:1: God looked into the Torah and created the world (amon of Proverbs 8:30).
Proverbs 3:18 sung when the Torah is returned to the ark.
Arius used LXX Proverbs 8:22 'created me'; Athanasius replied (Orations II); Nicaea 325 'begotten, not made', 'of one substance'.
claims.source: Athanasius, Orationes contra Arianos II; Nicene Creed

claims.claim: Colossians c. AD 60 if by Paul, or 70–90 by a disciple; 1:15–20 an early hymn.
Hebrews before c. AD 96, echoed by 1 Clement; Origen 'only God knows' the author.
Jesus prays Psalm 22:1 (Mark 15:34) and Psalm 31:5 (Luke 23:46); Luke 24:44; Hallel at Last Supper (Mark 14:26, probable).
Augustine: Christ prays for us as priest, in us as head, is prayed to by us as God.
Orthodox read the Psalter weekly in twenty kathismata; Rachmaninoff's All-Night Vigil (1915) sets Psalm 104 and Psalm 1.
Pontifical Biblical Commission (2001) calls the Jewish reading of the Bible 'possible'.
claims.source: The Jewish People and their Sacred Scriptures in the Christian Bible §22
